name: Panksepp primary-process emotional systems (and ANPS)

citation.title: Affective Neuroscience: The Foundations of Human and Animal Emotions

summary: Panksepp proposes that mammalian brains share a small set of evolutionarily ancient, subcortically organized primary-process emotional systems, each identifiable by localized electrical stimulation and neurochemistry. Unit of analysis is the neural emotional system (and, for the ANPS, the self-reported trait expression of each system in an individual). Panksepp & Biven (2012, The Archaeology of Mind: Neuroevolutionary Origins of Human Emotions, W. W. Norton, ISBN 978-0-393-70731-1) rename PANIC as PANIC/GRIEF.

constructs.label: Primary-process emotional systems
constructs.notes: Capitalized convention is Panksepp's own. Seven systems confirmed via Wikipedia (secondary) citing the 1998 and 2012 books; the 1998 text labels the separation-distress system PANIC, the 2012 text PANIC/GRIEF.

Six primary scales map to SEEKING, FEAR, CARE, RAGE (as ANGER), PLAY, PANIC (as SADNESS); LUST is deliberately omitted. name: Damasio somatic marker hypothesis / emotions, feelings and the self

citation.title: The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex
citation.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, Series B, 351(1346), 1413-1420; PMID 8941953

summary: Bodily-state ('somatic') signals associated with prior emotional outcomes mark response options and bias reasoning and decision making, consciously or covertly, with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex as key substrate (Descartes' Error, 1994, Putnam; 1996 paper). The Feeling of What Happens (1999, Harcourt) distinguishes emotion (public, bodily) from feeling (private, mental) and feeling-a-feeling (conscious), and layers proto-self, core self/core consciousness and autobiographical self/extended consciousness. Unit of analysis is the organism's body-state representation in response to a stimulus.

constructs.label: Somatic marker
constructs.notes: Abstract (Europe PMC): 'marker' signals influence the processes of response to stimuli at multiple levels of operation, some conscious and some not; the hypothesis also posits an 'as-if body loop' (body-state simulation without actual bodily change; from knowledge).

links details and images to a particular moment or moments of phenomenal experience

name: Lazarus cognitive-motivational-relational appraisal theory and Ways of Coping
summary: Emotions arise from appraisal of the person-environment relationship for its significance to well-being: primary appraisal (is this relevant to my goals?) and secondary appraisal (what can be done?). Each emotion corresponds to one core relational theme summarizing the harm or benefit. Coping (Lazarus & Folkman 1984, Stress, Appraisal, and Coping, Springer) is problem-focused or emotion-focused and is measured as process by the Ways of Coping Questionnaire (Folkman & Lazarus 1988, Consulting Psychologists Press). Unit of analysis is the appraised person-environment encounter.

constructs.label: Core relational themes (Lazarus 1991, p. 122 table)
values: Anger: a demeaning offense against me and mine
Fright: facing an immediate, concrete, and overwhelming physical danger
Guilt: having transgressed a moral imperative
Shame: having failed to live up to an ego-ideal
Sadness: having experienced an irrevocable loss
Envy: wanting what someone else has
Jealousy: resenting a third party for loss or threat to another's affection
Disgust: taking in or being too close to an indigestible object or idea (metaphorically speaking)
Happiness: making reasonable progress toward the realization of a goal
Pride: enhancement of one's ego-identity by taking credit for a valued object or achievement, either our own or that of someone or group with whom we identify
Relief: a distressing goal-incongruent condition that has changed for the better or gone away
Hope: fearing the worst but yearning for the better
Love: desiring or participating in affection, usually but not necessarily reciprocated
Compassion: being moved by another's suffering and wanting to help

name: McAdams narrative identity / life story model
summary: Identity in late adolescence and adulthood takes the form of an internalized, evolving life story that integrates the reconstructed past and imagined future to give life unity and purpose (McAdams 2001; McAdams & McLean 2013, 'Narrative Identity', Current Directions in Psychological Science 22(3), 233-238, DOI 10.1177/0963721413475622). Life stories are elicited with the Life Story Interview and coded for recurring themes and sequences. Unit of analysis is the narrated life-story episode (scene) and the themes coded across episodes.

constructs.label: Narrative identity constructs listed by McAdams & McLean (2013)
constructs.notes: Table 1 of McAdams & McLean 2013; Semantic Scholar verified title/year/DOI only. verified_against.title: McAdams (2018) Narrative identity: What is it? What does it do? How do you measure it? Imagination, Cognition and Personality 37(3) 359-372 (hosted on self-definingmemories.com)

A search snippet of the edX copy confirms Table 1 is headed 'Coding construct / Definition / Example (of high score)' with 'Agency' as its first row. Agency, communion, redemption, contamination and meaning making are confirmed as McAdams' coded constructs; 'exploratory narrative processing' and 'coherent positive resolution' (Pals 2006) are not confirmed by an accessible page - McAdams 2018 lists 'elaborative processing' and 'coherence' instead.
verified_against.note: Treat the last two labels as unverified.

constructs.label: Redemption sequence
constructs.notes: A demonstrably bad or emotionally negative scene turns into a good or positive outcome (McAdams, Reynolds, Lewis, Patten & Bowman 2001, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 27, 474-485). verified_against.title: Adler, Turner, Brookshier, Monahan, Walder-Biesanz, Harmeling, Albaugh, McAdams & Oltmanns (2015) Variation in narrative identity is associated with trajectories of mental health over several years, JPSP 108(3) 476-496 (PMC author manuscript)

verified_against.corrections: Definition confirmed. The subtypes in the note (sacrifice, recovery, growth, learning, improvement) were not confirmed: Foley Center instrument URLs (sesp.northwestern.edu/foley/instruments/...) all return 404 and no mirror of the redemption coding manual was found.
verified_against.note: McAdams et al. 2001 PSPB abstract not retrievable (PubMed search returned zero results; SAGE paywalled).

name: Bruner narrative mode and the narrative construction of reality
summary: Bruner (1986, Actual Minds, Possible Worlds, Harvard University Press) distinguishes two irreducible modes of thought: the paradigmatic (logico-scientific) mode that seeks truth through argument, and the narrative mode that seeks verisimilitude through story. The 1991 essay argues that narrative is a primary instrument by which humans construct and organize experience and reality, and enumerates ten features of narrative. Unit of analysis is the narrative (story) as a cognitive and cultural form.

constructs.notes: Actual Minds, Possible Worlds (1986), ch. 2.

verified_against.quote: There are two modes of cognitive functioning, two modes of thought, each providing distinctive ways of ordering experience, of constructing reality. ... One mode, the paradigmatic or logico-scientific one, attempts to fulfill the ideal of a formal, mathematical system of description and explanation. ... the logico-scientific mode (I shall call it paradigmatic hereafter)
verified_against.corrections: none

name: Tulving episodic vs semantic memory, autonoetic consciousness, encoding specificity

citation.title: Episodic memory: from mind to brain

summary: Tulving (1972, 'Episodic and semantic memory', in Tulving & Donaldson (eds.), Organization of Memory, Academic Press, pp. 381-403) distinguishes episodic memory for personally experienced events located in subjective time from semantic memory for general knowledge. Tulving (1985, 'Memory and consciousness', Canadian Psychology 26(1), 1-12, DOI 10.1037/h0080017) aligns procedural, semantic and episodic systems with anoetic, noetic and autonoetic consciousness; Tulving (2002) defines episodic memory as a uniquely human neurocognitive system enabling mental time travel, with chronesthesia as the capacity for subjective-time awareness. Unit of analysis is the memory system and the kind of conscious awareness accompanying retrieval.

constructs.label: Memory systems (monohierarchical)
constructs.notes: Tulving 1985: episodic is embedded in semantic, which is embedded in procedural.

verified_against.title: Slotnick & Schacter (2007) The cognitive neuroscience of memory and consciousness, in Zelazo, Moscovitch & Thompson (eds) Cambridge Handbook of Consciousness, pp. 809-827 (Harvard-hosted PDF)
verified_against.quote: Tulving (1985a) argued that each of three dissociable memory systems is uniquely associated with a particular type of consciousness. Specifically, he contended that procedural memory (learning of motor, perceptual, and cognitive skills) ... semantic memory (general factual knowledge) ... and episodic memory (recollection of personal experiences)
verified_against.corrections: none for the three systems. The 'monohierarchical' embedding (episodic within semantic within procedural) is not stated on any accessible page; it rests on the 1985 article itself (Canadian Psychology 26(1) 1-12, DOI 10.1037/h0080017), which is closed-access (alicekim.ca mirror 404).
